segments.text: Statistical inference uses sample data (and the sampling-distribution theory of Chapter 6) to draw formal conclusions about an unknown population — the two main tools, estimation and hypothesis testing, are two sides of the same inferential coin, and this chapter is arguably the practical core of the entire subject.

provides a range, calculated from sample data, expected to contain the true population parameter with a stated confidence level (commonly 95%). Critically, the correct interpretation is procedural, not about any single interval: a 95% confidence level means that if the same sampling and interval-construction procedure were repeated many times, approximately 95% of the resulting intervals would contain the true parameter — it is not correct to say there is a 95% probability the true (fixed) parameter lies within one specific, already-calculated interval.

A hypothesis test never directly “proves” the null hypothesis true — it can only fail to reject it (insufficient evidence against it) or reject it (sufficient evidence against it, in favour of the alternative) — this careful, asymmetric wording matters for correct interpretation and is frequently tested directly.

items.text: Point estimates give a single value; interval estimates (confidence intervals) additionally convey precision, and are generally preferable when available.
A good estimator is unbiased (correct on average) and has low variance (consistent across samples); these two properties together define efficiency.
A confidence interval’s correct interpretation is about the long-run reliability of the procedure across repeated sampling, not a probability statement about one already-calculated interval.
Hypothesis testing never proves the null hypothesis; it can only fail to reject it or reject it in favour of the alternative, based on the strength of sample evidence.

Type I error (false positive, rate α) and Type II error (false negative, rate β, related to power) trade off against each other for fixed sample size; only increasing sample size reduces both simultaneously.
Choosing between z, t, chi-square, and F-type procedures depends on the parameter of interest and whether relevant quantities (like variance) are known or must be estimated.
